en: The *Hūṃkāra-vidhi*, Part One:
The Vajrajñāna;
*Mañjuśrī-mañjughoṣa-ratnagarbha-hūṃkāra-devatā-sūkṣma-sādhana-mantra-yoga-japa-vidhi*. Chapter on the Maṇḍala: *Mañjuśrī-mañjughoṣa-ratnagarbha-hūṃkāra-devatā-sūkṣma-sādhana-mantra-yoga-japa*.
The Ritual Manual for Recitation: Chapter One, on the Maṇḍala. At that time, the King of the Hūṃ-kāra Gāthās, the Treasure-Storehouse of Much Learning, addressed all sentient beings, saying:
"I shall protect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
To provide protection for all sentient beings within the three realms,
and furthermore, to guard those in the five-turbulence evil world of Jambudvīpa— whether they be monastic bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs or lay upāsakas and upāsikās.
There is a great *dhāraṇī* method,
together with a great binding verse-mantra for all evils,

named the Root Universal Mantra, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Mantra, the Great Prohibitive Binding, the Great Secret Mantra that Accomplishes All Matters, the Great Prohibitive Binding *Hūṃ-kāra-ja*, and the Corresponding Wrathful Verse-Mantra.
If there are sons or daughters of good family,
or even animals and others,
who hear the names of these true mantras and my own name.
Take refuge in this Dharma.
By reciting and upholding the mantras and secret mudrās,
one shall not be afflicted by any calamities or illnesses throughout all successive lifetimes.
They will not be born in evil lands;
they will not be born to suffer the torments of the eighteen hells;
and they will not encounter immeasurable enemies.
They shall constantly encounter virtuous friends and spiritual teachers,
practice the Buddha-way,
and attain immeasurable merit and virtue.
Having attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment through sovereign cultivation,
King Bahuśruta therefore teaches the Dharma of universal prostration for the sake of all sentient beings.
That mudrā is the vajra-joined palms (*vajra-añjali*).
The mantra for universal prostration is:
Oṃ katha hūṃ nadini svāhā. Next is the mudrā for the self-confession.
Form the inner-bound fists with both hands.

Stand each *vāyu* (wind) finger upright; place the base of the right *vāyu* upon the left *vāyu*, and let it rest for about seven counts from top to bottom. This immediately purifies the three karmas.
The mantra for this is as follows:
Oṃ namo samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ vadamodana gaurīśaya hūṃ. By means of this mudrā and mantra, [one should act].
All impurities of the three karmas are completely eliminated.
Attaining the ocean of the Buddhas' wisdom is the intent of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Next, one should form the mudrā for entering the samaya and protecting the body of the noble Hūṃkārakrodha.
This is the perfection of diligence in its entirety.
For that mudrā, join the two hands in *añjali*,
with the two ring fingers placed side by side within the palms.
The two fire elements do not support one another;
the two wind elements and the two fire elements are joined back-to-back in the shape of a hook, remaining motionless as the two earth elements stand side by side.
The two space elements enter within and stand together.
Perform the ritual of expelling obstacles and establishing the boundary, and seal the five locations.
These five locations are: the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat.
Then, seal and draw [the mudrā] upward to the crown of the head, and finally disperse it over the heart.
One should then contemplate this seal as having the appearance of a great mass of fire,
and visualize the syllable *ra*.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām. Oṃ. Jūḥ sa-raṃ. Oṃ vaiśramaṇāya. Oṃ ku-ṭi-vī-de-dhi-jñi. Hūṃ jñi-lu. Svāhā. By means of this secret mudrā method.

All evil karma and grave offenses committed through the actions of body, speech, and mind— including the sin of slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the Mahāyāna sūtras, equal to that of an icchantika—
are entirely eliminated by relying on this seal-mantra.
Furthermore, in all places of foul odor and impurity,
by relying on this vidyā-dharma,
all that is unclean is completely eliminated.
One attains the yoga of pure activity.
Then, reciting this *hūṃ-kāra-ja* mantra, one binds the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Great Arising of Wisdom from the Secret Treasury, which has one face and ten hands.
If this seal and mantra are bound even once, [the result is attained].
Then, throughout immeasurable births in life after life, they shall not fall into evil states,
but shall always encounter the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Having heard the Dharma, one attains the ultimate fruit.
Next, one may form the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) corresponding to all matters:
with both hands... [gesture].
The two great elements enter within;
the two winds form the shape of jewels;
the two spaces and the truths lie side by side.
Without offering the wind [breath],
one immediately seals the five places and contemplates the syllable HŪṂ at the crown of the head.
The heart-mantra for that is:
Oṃ jñīḥ lūḥ svāhā. By recollecting this mantra and the power of its mudrā, all inauspicious influences such as the vināyakas will be dispelled.
That people do not approach is the Great Wisdom Seal (Mahājñānamudrā) of all Tathāgatas.
These three dharmas are the samayas of the three families of this very dharma.
First is the mantra for purifying one's own body, which is the Dharmagarbha-mudrā;
next is the vidyā of the Fire-light Mudrā,
the secret treasury of all the devas.
This is precisely the *saṃghāya*.
Next, the mantra of the Mind-Seal (*cittamudrā*) is this entire treasury of all Buddhas;
thus, the practitioner’s body attains the vajra-body.
The mantra for consecrating the perfumed water is:
HŪṂ VIKṚTADAṆḌA TUDAGAṬA SAṄNI HŪṂ DUBO SĀSĀ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. Having taken up the vajra and consecrated it, the mantra for scattering and sprinkling the water is:
HŪṂ 1 HŪṂ 2 HŪṂ 3 HŪṂ 4. One may recite this great mantra and perform the mudrā of summoning toward the maṇḍala to firmly bind away all inauspiciousness. The verse says:
OṂ Vajra-agra-dhāna-tāryāya (1) namo viśvamaṇe (2) śūra-vīra (3) mātara-ye (4) śvara (5) tvaṃ mahā (6).
Sattvaye hūṃ āra āradhmani oṃ maṇi maṇi kṣipta ra ra ra ra bhaya trātāre mahākālaye kṣetra hūṃ.
Tāraya (14) praviśa oṃ tiṣṭha pāyaya (15) oṃ (16) vaśita huṃ tāya (17) praveśaya (18) namaḥ (19).
[Recite] for that land, that province, that country,
that monastery, and for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, and so forth.
I, [Name], with a sincere heart,
entreat all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods and ten directions, as well as all vidyārājas,
śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of worthy and holy ones.
The celestial-dwelling and earth-dwelling protectors of the Dharma, the Four World-Protecting Kings and their twelve devas,
the various spirit-kings of the four directions and four corners, all the ghost kings, and the hosts of great yakṣa generals.
Without forsaking their original vows,
they come into the maṇḍala to bear witness to and certify the various ritual practices being performed.
Therefore, I, [Name], a bhikṣu (or bhikṣuṇī), with a sincere heart, request that you turn toward me and accept my prostrations: *Namo* to each of the four *Siddha-hūta-yas* of the East;
*Namo* to the assembly of the eight great *maṇḍala* realms and assemblies.
Homage to the various ghost-king generals of the east, each leading eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals;
to the various ghost-king generals of the south, each leading eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals;
and to the various ghost-king generals of the west, each leading eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals.
In the north, each leads eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals;
in the center, each leads eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals;
and each great deity leads a host of eighty-four thousand ghost-king generals and their retinues.
Namo! May the path of Dantālī in the east be severed;
may the path of Dantālī in the south be severed;
may the path of Dantālī in the west be severed.
The path to Uttarakuru in the north is severed;
the path to Aparagoyānī in the center is severed;
the path to Mahādeva in Uttarakuru is severed.
Namo to the Kālakālas of the east,
the Kālakālas of the south,
and the Kālakālas of the west.
Kara-kara in the north;
the great deity Kara-kara in the center;
homage to the Eastern King of Ghost Spirits, Nātha.
The Nātha King of Ghosts of the southern direction.
The Nātha King of Ghosts of the western direction.
The Nātha King of Ghosts of the northern direction.
The Central Nātha Gīśvara King and the Great Deity Nātha Gīśvara King stand at each of the four directions throughout the ten quarters; it is likewise for all others.
Homage to the assembly of noble Dharma protectors,
Maheśvara, the gods of the Heaven of Satisfaction, the twenty-eight lunar mansions,
the host of guardian deities, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three,
the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
and the Heaven of Contentment.
The Heaven of Delighting in Transformations,
the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations,
and the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly.
The Brahmapurohita Heaven,
the Mahābrahmā Heaven,
and the Parīttābha Heaven.
The Heaven of Immeasurable Light,
the Heaven of Ultimate Light,
and the Heaven of Limited Purity.
The Śubhakṛtsna devas,
the Apramāṇaśubha devas,
and the Vaśavartin devas.
The Heaven of No Sorrow,
the Heaven of No Affliction,
and the Heaven of No Heat.
The Heaven of the Birth of Merit,
the Heaven of Vast Results,
and the Heaven of Good Vision.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven,
and the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven.
The gods of the sphere of nothingness,
the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the twenty-eight lords who provide protection.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa,
the protector of the three realms, the steadfast Lord of the Earth,
and the Great General Samantabhadra.
The five hundred female attendants of Kālidī,
Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada,
and the Great General Ratnabhadra.
To the yakṣa general Saṃjñeya,
homage to the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
and to the Caṇḍāla spirits.
As well as the Kinnara King,
the Dragon King Anavatapta,
and the Śaṅkhapāla King.
The Asura King, the Garuḍa King,
and the Great Eloquence Deva.
And Mahāpuṇyadharā; such were the principal deities among the various celestial beings,
including Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods of the sun and moon.
King Yama, the various deities of wind and water,
and the Vaiśravaṇa devas.
As well as Viṣṇu,
the deity Mahāmati, and Maheśvara.
The great deities and others, the powerful and valiant great kṣetrapāla kings, Nārāyaṇa,
and all the various spirits and ghosts.
Led by Sanzhi,
there were hundreds of thousands of ghosts and spirits,
including the great ghost-king spirit Maṇibhadra.
Pūrṇabhadra, Vajrarājakapila, Āḷavaka,
and the yellow-headed deity Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.
Each of these deities has five hundred attendant spirits and ghosts.
As for the asura king Citta-sena:
And the gandharvas, nāgas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, śibis, and the golden-haired deva-king;
the bhūtas, pretas,
and the lords of the piśācas.
The Great Rain Deity,
the Great Food-and-Drink Deity,
and Mahāgaṭṭhila-palāsa, the Vānari deity of great majesty and power.
The yakṣa Dharmadruma-makhasara-śūciloma,
Śūli-mitra-leṇeśvara-mahābha, and Skandha-cañcā-maśati.
Furthermore, there are the great deities Śarabhaṇḍī,
Himavat, and Sātāgirī.
Namo natadāya. Namo jitāṃśubhāsurakṣitaprabha. Oṃ vā vajrakumāra.
The Dragon King Ekākṣara-śikhin,
the youth Licchavi,
and their retinue of five hundred and eighty million.
Their names were the youth Siṃhaprabha,
the youth Siṃhamati, and the youth Dharmadatta.
The youth Indra, the youth Mahāprabha,
and the youth Mahācaṇḍa.
The youth Buddhagupta,
the youth Dharmagupta,
and the youth Saṃghagupta.
The youth Vajrapāla, the youth Gaganapāla,
and the youth Gaganarāja.
To the youth Ratnagarbha, the youth Śrīgarbha,
and the ten rākṣasīs, etc., I pay homage.
All the great generals of the messengers,
with sincere hearts, firmly bind the celestial deities and firmly bind the earth deities.
Firmly bind the deities of the four directions and four corners;
firmly bind the vidyā-deities;
firmly bind the great deities.
Bind fast the minor spirits!
Bind fast the malevolent spirits!
Bind fast all evil ghosts!
Firmly bind all enemies and wicked persons!
Firmly bind the wicked persons; decisively subdue them!
Bind, bind! Firmly bind, firmly bind!
Oṃ vāsira jīvāpaya bhoḥ bhoḥ svāhā (with a long-drawn-out *laṅkāra* sound).
The mudrā is the vajra-fist.
Placing [the hands] upon each knee,
one stares with wide-open eyes toward the four directions.
If there is anyone who recites and maintains this verse-mantra, [they shall be protected].
This person eliminates the one hundred and eight afflictions as well as the sixty-two views,
attaining immeasurable merit and sovereign mastery. Why is this so?
This mantra is praised by all Buddhas;
from this mantra arises the dharma of my own mind.
This great dhāraṇī verse subdues all evil matters.
When reciting this verse,
one should bring to mind the various great malevolent beings, the Vināyakas, the great evil spirits, the kings of the gods,
and the various non-Buddhists.
The deities of heaven and earth, the four quarters, and the hosts of malevolent spirits,
as well as all the great and small gods within the realm,
are all completely bound and restrained.
If the practitioner’s mind within becomes agitated during recitation, they should repeatedly draw out the sound of *krodha* (wrath) to subdue it.
Upon finishing the recitation, they should then contemplate the syllables *HŪṂ*, *RA*, and *KHAṂ*.
The mantra for sprinkling purification (*prokṣaṇa*) is as follows:

Oṃ digamgaya hūṃ. Sphoṭakākhya. If one wishes to practice this rite, one should first select and seek out a location before a Buddha statue, before a stūpa, in a monastic dwelling, by a riverbank, beneath a forest tree, or in a forest hermitage (araṇya).
Furthermore, that which the mind delights in as a place free from obstacles is the supreme siddhi;
this is the practice for those who cultivate mantras.
One should first cause the skull, dead bones, shards, stones, and other such foul, painful, and impure objects to be removed. Thereafter,
the practitioner proceeds to a pure location,
takes pure earth, and constructs a mandala altar and so forth.
Thereafter, one should practice the mantra methods.
When taking up the earth, [one should do so with the following visualization].
The Buddha division is empowered by means of mantras.
Thereafter, take earth to construct the mandala;
for the pacifying (śāntika) rite, the mandala is circular.
The *pauṣṭika* rite [uses] a square with four corners;
the *ābhicāruka* rite [uses] one with eight corners;
each is made to be eight cubits in size.
Furthermore, one may construct it with five or three cubits.
The mantra for consecrating the ground of the maṇḍala is:
Oṃ natha natha jñāna jñāna nandapari svāhā. If there is anyone who upholds this mantra method, [they shall attain success].
When constructing the altar, first recite this mantra one hundred and eight times to consecrate the ground;
thereby all insects, ants, and other species will move away and take refuge elsewhere.
Upon attaining that, it is immediately purified;
this concludes the preparation of the site for the altar.
One then constructs the eight great maṇḍalas of the Great Dharma.
Their names were: first, the Maṇḍala-realm of Single Cause;
second, the Maṇḍala-realm of Entering the Dharma;
third, the Maṇḍala-realm of Entering Characteristics.
4. The maṇḍala realm of the four entries into the treasury;
5. The maṇḍala realm of the wondrous treasury;
6. The maṇḍala realm of realization and entry.
The seventh is the realm of the Maṇḍala of Perfect Dharma;
the eighth is the realm of the Corresponding Maṇḍala.
These are called the eight great maṇḍala realms.
These are the eight great maṇḍalas.
Regarding the explanation of each one's name:
as for the term *maṇḍala*, it is because—
This is the seed maṇḍala.
It is the dharma-entry maṇḍala.
That is, the great maṇḍala has three types, including the hearth-altar.
Entering the mandala of marks:
while the practitioner performs the homa,
they should mentally visualize the physical form and characteristics of the Honored One.
Furthermore, one should glare with eyes wide open while recollecting the essence of the Buddha’s state;
this is precisely the visualization of the maṇḍala.
As for entering the treasury maṇḍala:
This refers to the arrangement and appearance of the retinues and classes of deities,
such as Śrī-devī and others. Specifically,
it refers to Śrī-devī herself along with her assembly of nine celestial maidens.
The world-realm *Sugata-garbha* (妙藏世界) is none other than *Mandala*.
All these honored ones have gathered from their respective realms and taken their seats,
established according to their original positions.
One who has accomplished the dharma to be practiced and whose perception of this realm is vivid and perfectly clear is called an ācārya;
one who does not clearly perceive this realm is not called an ācārya.
This very realm accomplishes the world;
this very realm is named the Maṇḍala of Turning the Wheel of Dharma;
it is the realm of realization and entry.
This is the seat of the yakṣa great generals such as Dūta and others.
It is the circular world-realm (*maṇḍaladhātu*).
This refers to King Vaiśravaṇa, his two celestial consorts, and the eight-tusked deities associated with wrath.
The corresponding world consists of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, Śākyamuni, the four thousand Akṣobhya-Vajrapāṇis, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and so forth;
these are called the Eight Great Maṇḍalas.
The practitioner should first visualize the eight great worlds;
their characteristics should first be visualized according to the ritual rules.
Then, one completes the mandala in this manner.
Next, one contemplates the world of the Perfect Dharma with the mind.
First, one visualizes the central principal figure, the body of Vaiśravaṇa,
wearing armor adorned with the seven precious jewels and vajras.
His left hand cradles a stūpa,
and his right holds a trident;
beneath his feet, he treads upon three yakṣa demons.
The central principal deity is named Bhūmidevī,
also known as Nandādevī;
those at her left and right are named the Messenger Maidens (Dūtī).
The one on the left is named the goddess Nīlāmbā;
the one on the right is named the divine king Vīrāmba.
These three spirits have faces that look toward one another, possessing excellent features and bodies.
The female deities on the left and right possess all the marks and signs of excellence.
Furthermore, beneath the seat are five great sons,
each acting as a general and clad in armor and helmets.
Each hand holds a bow and arrow;
furthermore, there are celestial maidens of the Five Paths who are clad in armor and helmets.
Her facial features and female form are fully perfected;
furthermore, she holds a sickle and a knife in her hands.
Moreover, this goddess exists.
Furthermore, they are clad in armor;
their faces are contorted with rage,
and in their hands they hold swords and sickles.
Each sat upon a stone seat;
these are known as the assembly of the ten great generals.
The auspicious goddess Śrī possesses perfect and excellent marks.
Her various garments and ornaments are beyond compare.
The celestial maiden holds a blue lotus in her left hand,
while her right hand displays the mudrā of granting fearlessness.
The crown is adorned with the five precious jewels;
the eyes possess the marks beloved by King Vaiśravaṇa;
the face is fine, fair, and slightly ruddy; and she dwells upon a lotus petal.
There are nine women of the retinue,
as well as Śrīdevī, whose auspicious marks are peerless in the world;
each holds a precious sword in her hand.
Furthermore, they carry spears and hold mirrors;
three persons each hold these objects.
Each resides upon a lotus petal.
Furthermore, those with eight prongs stand facing backward;
their facial color is red.
The color of his garment is black;
each face has three eyes,
or if it is half [a face], it has three eyes.
If one has two eyes, the upper teeth extend one finger-width beyond the lower teeth;
the white teeth are long, and the lower teeth beneath the armpits each measure one finger-width across the chest.
With both hands joined together below the navel, one forms the *añjali* mudrā.
In one hand, join the palms above;
join the palms below while holding a khaṭvāṅga;
and join the palms above while holding a vajra.
He sits upon a circular seat;
his head bears the mark of a heavenly crown,
and his hair is styled with locks turned upward and hanging down.
Each face has a most terrifying appearance;
seeing them causes people to feel revulsion and confusion.
Among the nine men who lead the host, all have long fangs.
Each is clad in armor,
their faces terrifying,
and each resides upon a lotus petal.
The upper fangs are short;
the lower fangs are long,
extending beyond the seat.
Each holds a bow and arrow in hand;
the Lord of Great Learning is in the center,
and the Auspicious King is in the north.
To the south of King Aṣṭadanta, each [is attended by] a host of devas;
to the east, the seats of the Devendra-rājas and others; and to the west.
In the northeast corner is Maheśvara;
next is Śakra; next is Agni.
They have the appearance of aged men;
their bodies are red in color.
Next, they are all [accompanied by] the god Īśvara.
Yama-deva; next, Rāhu-deva;
next, Varuṇa-deva.
Next, together with the Brahmā devas;
next, the Earth devas;
next, together with the Wind devas.
First the Sun Deity,
next the Moon Deity,
and next the Heavenly King Mahākāla.
Together there are twelve heavens;
all have stone seats and dwellers clad in armor.
Each hand holds a trident knife;
however, the Fire King (Agni) alone holds a water flask in his first hand and a bamboo staff in his second, with the characteristic of flames encircling his body.
This is what is called the "Entrance into the Treasury" maṇḍala.
Furthermore, one completes the Dharma-maṇḍala.
The practitioner clearly perceives the wisdom of the Buddha-stage within this world;
even the construction of the maṇḍala is performed in this manner.
First, for the body mudrā of King Vaiśravaṇa:
first join the two hands in *añjali*;
then insert the index and middle fingers (*vāyu* and *tejas*) into the palms.
Pointing toward the earth, fire, space, and each direction respectively,
one establishes the boundaries in the five directions above and the four directions below.
By recollecting this mudrā and its empowerment, all obstacles and difficulties— such as the Vināyakas and other malevolent spirits— are entirely driven away.
One cannot harm such a practitioner;
all that they seek shall be accomplished,
and they will immediately attain a body endowed with extensive learning and wisdom.
That consort said:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ māyā svāhā*. Next is the mudrā of the goddess Śrī:
with both hands, form the inner-binding (*muṣṭi-bandha*).
Each wind-finger stands extended;
by reciting [the mantra] over each breast, all wishes are immediately fulfilled.
The milk-ocean flows forth entirely from the practitioner’s body through the power of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Bestowed upon all sentient beings,
it becomes an excellent medicine for those who are ill,
and it becomes a means of fulfillment for those who have expectations.
If for those suffering from famine, it becomes food and drink;
if for those who are impoverished, it becomes jewels, clothing, and food;
and if for those who have no wife, no husband, or no servants, it likewise becomes each respective benefit.
This very Ocean of Milk has such characteristics that it can be visualized; its mantra is:
Oṃ mahāśrī-devī svāhā. Next is the seal of the nine attendants and celestial maidens.
Each forms the inner-binding mudrā;
each of the wind and fire [elements] should be extended upward and adjusted.
Perform the dance three times to the left and right in the manner of joyful delight.
One should then think: "I shall bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings;
these messengers are all my emissaries.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ mahāvajra dvitīyadeva vi svāhā. Next is the mudrā of Aṣṭadaṃṣṭra:
join the two hands in the inner-binding (*antarbaddha*), extend each index finger (*vāyu-aṅguli*) from below toward the knees, and pull them down three times.
One should then contemplate the mark of the long fangs and the mark of subduing all corresponding māras.
The mantra is: Oṃ hiliye tara hūṃ svāhā. Next are the mudrās of the nine Great Generals and their retinues.
Each forms a fist at the heart;
with eyes narrowed in a wrathful gaze, they behold the honored image and contemplate the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, these nine persons are all youths who practice this path of the self.
Recite the mantra for that deity:
Oṃ tathāgata-vajra-dhṛte svāhā. Next is the general mudrā of the twelve great devas.
The two hands are joined in *añjali*;
the two fire-teeth are reclined;
this is the seal of the five places.
The mantra is as follows:

*Manasparśanāmadheyam* (1) *Oṃ* (2) *Iṣṭārāya* (3) *Agrye* (4) *Dhṛtijaye* (5) *Vāruṇye* (6) *Pavitrīye* (7) *Anityakantārāya* (8) *Oṃ Mahākālīye* (9) *Svāhā* (10). One should visualize this within the mandala realm.
The practitioner then dwells within the pure dharma-realm,
recollecting Mahāvairocana Tathāgata,
who is adorned with a crown of five jewels upon his head.
Adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
his facial features are perfect and auspicious;
he forms the mudrā of meditative concentration.
Upon the great lotus king-throne,
next to the south is Maitreya Bodhisattva,
holding a single-pronged and a triple-pronged vajra.
Adorned with a jeweled crown and necklaces,
endowed with all auspicious marks,
and seated upon a wondrous lotus throne.
Next, to the south, is the four-armed Acala;
his color is deep blue with long, hanging hair,
and he possesses a most terrifying appearance like surging waves.
With the right hand facing forward, he holds a chain-noose; with the left, he holds a lasso.
Next, the left hand holds a lotus flower;
next, the right hand holds a precious jewel.
Seated upon a Mount Sumeru throne,
his body was encircled by a halo of fire,
and he was fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
With an incomparable wrathful expression, next to the north is Śākyamuni Buddha;
his uṣṇīṣa is visible upon his crown,
and his dharma robes encircle his body.
He displays the mudrā of preaching the Dharma;
newly manifesting the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics in their full perfection,
he sits upon a sublime lotus-king throne.
Next, in the north, there is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
adorned with a precious crown and manifesting precious necklaces;
his left hand holds a lotus flower.
The right hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*),
and there is a blue lotus seat;
even the construction [of the rest] is likewise performed in this manner.
First is the Wisdom Seal (jñānamudrā) of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata;
next is the mantra,
which is the General Seal (samudramudrā) of the corresponding realm.
With vajra-gold palms joined above the head, one spreads the robe in all directions while reciting the mantra and mudrā for donning the armor of all Tathāgatas.
That vidyā-mantra is: Oṃ vajra-dhara hūṃ trātrā svāhā. Next, one visualizes entering the world of the maṇḍala.
In the central capital city, the Lord of the North,
Vaiśravaṇa, dwells atop Mount Mi;
at the foot of the mountain, there are three yakṣī-demonesses.
The Great Heavenly King wears a massive great sword at his waist;
he has a bull’s head on the eastern side,
which is extremely terrifying to behold.
On the crown of the head is the eleven-faced form of Bhairava;
from each of the horns, ornaments emerge.
Furthermore, there is one face on each side of the central face.
Furthermore, his fearful aspect is that of the deity Śakra;
he dwells upon a lotus leaf.
With his left hand he holds a large *mūṣala* (pestle),
and with his right hand he wields a great sword.
To the left is the Vajragarbha King Deity, who has a cow's head and faces forward.
He sits in the squatting posture upon a celestial golden bed,
wearing armor and the attire characteristic of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
With palms joined,
the hair upon his head ascends into the heavens and blazes with fire;
on his left side, a great spear stands upright in the earth.
To the left of the seat is bestowed the Deity-King of the Auspicious Ghosts (*Puṇyabhūta-rājā*).
He has the form of a great ghost and is naked;
his hair is ablaze with fire, and with his left hand he draws it upward from his head.
With his right hand, he holds a large staff over his shoulder;
the deity of the King of Treasuries (Gopaka) acts out of reverence,
while the Heavenly King who is the Lord of the Right Side with Ox Heads presides.
Fully adorned with a jeweled crown, necklaces, and celestial robes,
his physical form and features are identical to those of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
he dwells upon a four-petaled lotus flower.
This is the celestial form corresponding to Mahāvairocana Tathāgata.
His hand gesture is the *añjali* (palms joined).
He sits upon a seat, with the Kṣetrapāla deity at his lower right.
His physical form is like that of the deity Śubhavyūha;
however, his right hand grasps hair,
while his left hand holds a *pūrṇa-ghaṭa* (vase of plenty) upon his shoulder.
In the center of the southern direction, there are three figures to the right.
The first is the deity Mucilinda,
characterized by the appearance of wearing armor.
The left hand holds a bell;
the right hand holds a bell,
and the [other] right hand holds a five-pronged vajra.
Next, he returns to the Sūdaya heaven;
with his left hand he takes the bell,
and with his right hand he takes the trident.
Next is the deity Paricita;
his left and right hands hold three-pronged vajras.
Next, the central principal deity on the left side is the northern deity, Phelipa (Phelipa).
The right hand holds a sword;
the left hand holds a golden *kṣurikā*.
Next is King Maudgalyāyana.
A staff in the right hand and a sword in the left;
next is King Vighnāntaka,
holding a long spear in his left hand.
The aforementioned six heavens all have stone seats upon which they stand.
Next is the central mistress, the goddess of superior practice.
Seated upon a golden bed like an auspicious woman,
she holds a casket in her left hand.
The jewel is in her right hand.
To her right is the first noble attendant goddess,
holding a spear in her left hand and a shield in her right.
Next, proceed to the deity Sūvarṇa;
his attendants hold tridents,
and to his left is the one-handed Ḍākinī, Han Tian.
The left and right hands form fists;
each has a fang positioned at the chest, with the intention of standing upright like a spear on the left side.
Next is the attendant deity, Seishōten (Viśvadeva).
The right hand holds a blade and the left a spear.
Next, in the northeast corner of the four directions, is the Heavenly King Kārttikeya;
his left hand holds a bow and his right two arrows.
Next is the deity of Light-Radiance (Ābhāsvara),
standing with palms joined and holding a spear in his left hand.
Next is the deity of the Lord of Māras (Māra-rāja).
Holding a spear in the left hand and a sword in the right, he has not yet descended to the ground.
Next is King Kumbhīra,
holding a sword in his left hand and a club in his right.
To the left stands a spear;
next is the Heavenly King Deṭa,
holding a bow in his left hand and an arrow in his right.
The left *kunta* stands upright.
Next is the deity of the residence, *Śakra*,
holding a bow in his left hand held horizontally across his chest.
Holding an arrow in his right hand,
and having performed such actions as these,
he immediately entered the world-system.
Beginning with King Liangshi and ending with the deity Zheshou Goutianwang,
all were seated in a squatting posture on the right side,
each clad in armor and mail.
With a face and features so hideous that people are struck with terror,
he is the Great General Śiva.
He is the universal seal for entering this world-realm.
Join the two palms together.
Separate the two index fingers and extend them upright;
this is the mudrā for sealing the five locations.
Contemplate that the Great General and the assembly have received empowerment and protection.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabhadranām oṃ takkaye svāhā*. Next, visualize the dharmas entering the body of the Honored One in the maṇḍala through the yoga of the image.
This is the body of the Great King Daśabhuja;
by means of this very body, the ultimate body of the mantra of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa is equal to the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana and all the other Honored Ones.
First, regarding their physical form:
the skin is red, the undergarment is dark blue,
and the *kāṣāya* robe is green.
The eyes are white.
The teeth measure three finger-widths above and below.
This is the *shushō-in* (correct hand seal).
Regarding that fundamental mudrā for protecting the body:
the second hand on the left side holds a precious stūpa,
while the next hand holds a trident-topped vajra and a bell.
Next, he holds a golden sickle;
next, he holds an arrow and a noose;
and in his second right hand, he holds a precious sickle.
Next, he holds a great sword in his hand;
next, he holds a bow in his hand;
next, he holds a *triśūla* and a spear.
He dwells atop Mount Sumeru;
below the mountain, he has the form of a ghost and stands on his left knee.
He lies on his right side with his knees drawn up;
the Four World-Protecting Heavenly Kings stand in respectful attendance,
though only the Northern Prince of Supreme Excellence is present.
The front face is upright and fully endowed with auspicious marks;
the left and right faces have fearsome expressions.
The face on the right side is red.
The left side is black;
the top of the head is red;
the face and throat are narrow and elongated.
The appearance is that of hair on fire.
With hands joined in the *añjali* mudrā,
the second fingers of both the left and right hands grasp a great sword.
Next, the third hands on both the left and right grasp tridents.
Next, the fourth hands on both the left and right hold spears.

From the mouths of the great nāga kings and their princes held in the left and right hands, vajra-wheels with equal sickles emerge; their tails extend downward, reaching halfway down to the feet of the prince.
While the Prince remained standing thus upon the rock,
there appeared twelve divine generals beneath King Huṅka;
their forms were exceedingly terrifying.
Clad in armor and each wielding swords and staves,
they were led by that foremost general, Kubera, or by one of the twelve great generals.
In the sequence of placement, there is the Great General Vajrapāṇi Samantajñānin;
his form is that of a powerful athlete, naked and of most terrifying aspect.
Samantajñānin is adorned with all manner of necklaces and ornaments, and he holds a weapon.
Next, there are ten rākṣasīs and others below;
their forms are extremely terrifying,
and they are clad in armor.
Each held a sword and staff;
their physical forms were upright and exceedingly beautiful, endowed with all the [auspicious] marks.
Each held a sword and staff in hand.
Having thus constructed the maṇḍala,
the practitioner of wisdom should contemplate each and every characteristic with mindfulness.
Now, following this pattern, their respective positions are listed in succession.
First, construct a three-tiered altar.
The first and second courtyards each have three internal divisions;
the third courtyard on the western side is elongated horizontally.
One should visualize five deities: first, Mahāvairocana Tathāgata;
in the north, Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
In the south is Maitreya Bodhisattva;
the four-armed Acala;
and in the center of the central court, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the Central Court.
Below are the ten great generals;
in the north is the Bodhisattva Mahāśrīdevī;
below her are nine celestial maidens.
In the south are the Eight Tusked Heavenly Kings,
together with their subordinates— the nine men and the host of Great General Long-Tusked Ones;
in the west are the Twelve Devas.
Furthermore, beyond the exterior to the north is King Madhyama-darbha;
to the east are King Gośīrṣa and King Vajra.
He also conferred upon them the titles of the Devas of the Auspicious Gods,
the Heavenly Kings, and the Official Deities:
in the south, the King of Manyāra, the Deva Viputrara, and the King of Ikura, Pratyāra-deva.
King Mitradeva;
the Northern Deva Dhanika;
and the attendant goddess Tārā.
The King Heaven of Rites,
the King Heaven of Many Hairs,
and the Heavenly King of Divine Footsteps.
In the center is the Sovereign Lord who has attained mastery over the celestial general’s army;
in the northwest corner is the deity Vakkulada; and [in the northeast corner] is the deity Saṃkusumita.
Māra-rāja, Tārāpati, and Kūmudakara-devendra.
The Sovereign King of Virtuous Attainment,
the Lord of the Celestial Abode, the General of Sovereign Power, and the Tārāṇī King—
these entered the maṇḍala from the Central Court of the East, the realm of the Wondrous Treasury Maṇḍala.
The four corners form a platform separated into three tiers, with a great diamond-jewel *kalaśa* at the central altar.
The four directions are marked by a cross-shaped *karma*-mandala.
In the second enclosure, there is a *kundikā* water-flask in the west.
In the south is a large three-pronged vajra;
in the north, a great dharma conch; in the east, a stupa shape.
In the third enclosure, in the east, is the lion king.
In the south is the Great Dragon King;
in the west, the Peacock Bird King;
and in the north, the Rākṣasa Form.
From within the four-cornered precious incense vases, lotus-shaped forms emerge;
these are called the Great Wheels in the world-realm of Wondrous Treasury (Ghanavyūha).
They are named the Four Great Honored Ones, the four cardinal directions of the十字王 (Cross-Wheel King) of Vairocana Tathāgata.
In the southern part of the second courtyard, the names of the three deities of the trident are as follows;
in the west, the kamaṇḍalu is named One Face Ten Arms King;
and in the north, the great dharma-conch is named the Sign of Transmitting the Wheel of Dharma.
The practitioner, abiding in this samādhi,
invites all the honored ones and presents offerings such as argha water.
This is the formation of the conch-seal (*śaṅkha-mudrā*).
One who recites my mantra of truth should blow this conch, vowing that all the Honored Ones shall propagate the Great Dharma Wheel.
The jeweled stupa in the eastern direction is the Great Dharma Treasury.
In the eastern part of the third courtyard are the great generals such as Siṃharāja (Lion King), who have realized the state of equality;
in the southern part are the one-faced, ten-armed Nāga King and all the nāga kings, appearing in the form of those who uphold and follow him.
The Western Bird King is the sign of the swift accomplishment of the Dharma;
the Northern Rākṣasa King is the sign of the subjugation of all inauspicious and evil matters by Vaiśravaṇa.
The practitioner is able to know the characteristics and forms of this maṇḍala.
While traversing this world,
they further perform the随心 (sui-xin) maṇḍala according to the Great Secret Mantra, along with the empowerment (abhiṣeka).
The practitioner, dwelling in this world,
then further creates the maṇḍala that accords with the mind,
and further creates the maṇḍala within the mind.

In sequence, outside the eastern enclosure, in the northern courtyard, there is a circular mandala. From its four sides emerge lotus kings, and from its four sides emerge three-pronged vajras. The front vajra is shaped like a lotus and is centered upon a cross; this is called the *śāntika* rite for entering the world.

Next, in the southern outer enclosure, construct a triangular mandala; from each of its three corners project a single-pronged vajra, and from the two sides project lotuses, with a single-pronged vajra at the center of the cross.
This is called the *abhicāruka* rite for entering the maṇḍala.
This is precisely the model for the eight great maṇḍalas.

When a practitioner of wisdom visualizes and constructs them in this manner, the deities will all arrive due to the causal conditions arising from that maṇḍala, which is the wondrous treasury of the world.
This ritual for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala is itself the yoga-maṇḍala.
When the practitioner attains contemplative wisdom, this world-appearance immediately accomplishes all dharmas, all great vows, and the seals (mudrā) of the noble ones.

The earth [mudrās] of the left and right are again placed face down upon the water, each entering into the palms of the left and right; with the empty [space] of each side, the water is not yet applied.
The fire fingers of the left and right are like pillars, slightly apart and not joined, forming a cross-like shape held upright.
Facing the direction of the Heavenly Altar, before the union has occurred, one should erect the mudrā at five locations.
The Great Mantra-jewel is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ | oṃ vajrasaraṇa-gata ṭhaḥ hūṃ jvala raṃ hūṃ svāhā*. By means of the empowerment of this mantra and mudrā, [the rite is accomplished].
The practitioner of mantra is identical in body to the body of a *sattva*;
do not harbor any further doubt.
The Buddhas do not withhold this merit.
If it becomes medicine for the sick,
or if it becomes a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) according to whatever object is required,
it is because it accomplishes all dharmas.
The mantra of the Cintāmaṇi-ratna is as follows: *Namo samantabuddhānām | mahā-āroṣya | oṃ viśva-saumyatarasajñāvara-karakiṅkuru-cūru-śaṇi | dharmadhātu svāhā.*
Each forms a vajra-fist;
each fire-finger and tooth enters into the palm, which is drawn up onto the knee.
One should then visualize it as a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi).
If those who uphold this Dharma give rise to thoughts of compassion toward all sentient beings,
they will harbor no mind of anger, deceit, flattery, or malice.
If one gives rise to anger, one immediately loses its great spiritual efficacy;
therefore, always guard the mind against malice.
Furthermore, when a person upholds this dharma-mantra...
Throughout each day, remember me—
the Sage of Great Learning— and my retinue, and offer them praise;
may we always assist one another through the ten wholesome actions.
I realized enlightenment;
having known this matter by recollecting those hosts of devas.
All were greatly rejoiced and came together to protect and uphold this person who recites the mantra, as well as those who maintain the vidyā-mantra.
Their lifespan shall be long-lasting, enduring for immeasurable eons;
they shall forever be free from the three miserable realms and always remain without calamity or misfortune. Furthermore, they shall cause them to obtain wish-fulfilling jewels and hidden treasures.
With mastery over supernormal powers,
all their aspirations will be fulfilled;
if they seek official rank or glory, there shall be nothing that does not accord with their wishes.
Furthermore, to understand the speech of all birds and beasts is a merit of the mantra.
A brief account of this is as follows.
If the practitioner wishes to perform the rite,
they should first prepare the ground for the maṇḍala;
first, with a straightforward mind, they should join their palms in añjali.
Entering the stage of samādhi with a concentrated mind free from all other thoughts,
one contemplates the nature of this stage:
first, there is a wheel of emptiness.
The seed syllable is adorned with a circle of various colors and a crescent shape.
Next, one visualizes the wind mandala,
which is black in color and shaped like a half-moon.
The syllable *Haṃ* (the union of *ha* and *aṃ*) serves as its seed-syllable.
Next, one should contemplate the fire-wheel,
which is triangular in shape and red in color.
The syllable *ra-a* (combined) is the seed-syllable.
Next, one should visualize a water-wheel,
which is the syllable *vaṃ*.
It is white in color and circular in shape.
Next, one contemplates the earth mandala,
which is square in form.
Yellow in color,
one should take the syllable A as its great seed-syllable;
this constitutes the mantra of the samādhi of contemplating that [deity] with mind and speech.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām* (1) *Oṃ* (2) *Khaṃ kṣaṃ laṃ vaṃ āḥ svāhā* (3). Next, one should visualize the ground of these eight great maṇḍalas.
This is precisely the indestructible world of the vajra,
the eternally abiding world of the various honored ones,
the pure dharma-realm.
From here, to the north of the Great Heavenly King, there is a city named Animanda.
That city is composed of the seven treasures; it is exceedingly indestructible, and the World-Honored Ones of all worlds constantly dwell therein—a wondrous world, peerless.
This Mahādeva dwells in this realm;
he beholds those who, having bound the mudrā,
recite the mantra without forsaking the samaya.
They will surely come to this maṇḍala;
the great vows of all sentient beings shall be fulfilled.
Then, recite the gāthā for the invitation:

Then he spoke in verse: "Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to the devas and others! I pray only that the Great King will look downward toward this place. By the power of looking downward, may you protect and uphold the mandala and so forth, so that all aspirations may be fulfilled. Furthermore, he bound the seal within the purified hall: the earth and water mudrās of the left and right hands were both inserted into the palms of their respective fingers.

Furthermore, one should point toward the sky for each respective direction, placing [the elements] between the earth and water of each direction; the fire on the left is originally placed on the left, while the end of the fire on the right is placed on the right.
Furthermore, when the left and right winds form the shape of a jewel-palace, it becomes pure within; then,
by sealing the five places according to this mantra-seal,
whatever one desires within the palace becomes entirely purified.
There shall be no calamities such as malevolent insects and the like. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, āpadita-gagana-samādhāni hūṃ phaṭ*. Next is the mudrā for the interior of the Jewel-Adorned Hall.
With the left and right hands, place the head [of the fingers] upon the *sthāpana* (placement) and move them back and forth according to the *vighna-ghātana-mantra*. The mantra is:
Oṃ samaya hūṃ. Next, perform the *trailokyavijaya-mudrā*: bind the left and right hands internally, interlace the earth (*pṛthivī*) and water (*ap*) fingers, and let them lie flat.
The two fire-heads stand upright together;
the two winds lie straight and horizontal on the left and right.
The tip of the right fire is joined with the space on the left.
Place the left hand with the fire-finger extended and the right hand with the space-finger placed upon it.
First seal the five locations,
and next release [the mudrā] into the center of the maṇḍala.
The mantra is:
*Namo samantabuddhānām āgneyadhuru hūṃ phaṭ*. Next, perform the mudrā for delimiting the boundary of the Four Great Heavenly Kings: with both hands, bend the little fingers into the palms.
The right hand presses down upon the left,
with the two middle fingers and ring fingers separated by one cun; the two index fingers are held upright,
and the two thumbs are both bent inward into the palms.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vadaya bandha haṃ hūṃ svāhā. By forming this mudrā, all evils are entirely dispersed and driven far away.
Perform this mudrā three times for both the upward and downward directions.
Next, bind the mudrā of the Four Heavenly Kings:
first, place the right hand on the waist with the vāyu-finger (the little finger) raised.
Press the little finger of the left hand against the thumb, extend the other three fingers upright, and place them upon the navel.
When reciting the mantra, one should manifest a wrathful expression with a malevolent intent.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ loka-pāleṣu jaya jaya jaye hūṃ svāhā. Using this mudrā and mantra, one invites the Four Heavenly Kings.
This is the seal for inviting the Supreme Protector from afar.
Next, form the seal for accomplishing the practice of Mahāśrīdevī-yoga:
join the two palms together.
Place the two thumbs side by side, about one cun away from the sides of the wind fingers (the index fingers).
Slightly curve the tips of the two little fingers so that they press against each other.
Bend the water and fire fingers (the middle and ring fingers) so that their tips are separated like the shape of a hook; thus it is formed.
The mantra of the Seven-Jeweled Kāmalā is:
Oṃ vimale viśalavati tsara hūṃ. Next, one should form the mudrās for the messengers, celestial maidens, and others.
Bend the right arm to cover the left, draw the neck back slightly behind the upper elbow, curve the body forward,
and reach toward the ground while reciting this mantra. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ ajagani dantira mañcaṭa hasi ca hūṃ phaṭ ca hūṃ ca. Forming this mudrā, one then invites the Vajradūtas, such as Devapila and others.
They were all filled with joy;
they went quickly to the place of the mantra-master,
whereupon they acted as they pleased.
All ritual actions will be fully accomplished.
Next, form the Samaya-seal for the invitation:
first, join the palms with the ten fingers interlaced, the tips pointing inward.
The two water [elements] stand upright with their heads touching.
The two wind [elements] stand upright, slightly bent; the left [wind] enters the right palm to press down upon the left fire-nail.
The right [wind] passes over the back of the left [wind] to enter the left palm to press down upon the fire-nail.
The two winds follow the sound of *ha* and summon one another.
When the true mind maintains this seal-method,
it is the seal for inviting and summoning the assembly of the realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The mantra is:
Namo samanta-buddhānām (1) Oṃ (2) Oṃ (3) Vaiśravaṇāya (4) Hihī (5) Svāhā (6). With this mudrā and by reciting the mantra seven times, [one achieves the desired result].
The retinue of the Heavenly King descended upon the ritual arena.
The Heavenly King, out of compassion, took his seat and accepted the modest offerings. As for those invited from among his attendants, each took their respective seats.
Having accepted my offerings,
he immediately knelt on his right knee, took the incense burner in his hand,
and with a sincere heart invoked all the yakṣas and rākṣasas who constitute his retinue before the Heavenly King.
Furthermore, may the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas such as Vairocana and Śākyamuni, along with the Vajrapāṇis, descend upon this site of practice to bear witness for me.
This is the site of practice of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.
One attains the methods of accomplishment,
the supernormal powers of the body,
and great mastery.
May all your wishes be fulfilled according to your heart's desire.
Next is the seal of food and drink:
bind the left and right hands in the inner-binding gesture.
Pointing the tips of the fingers upward so that they touch one another,
extend the left and right hands inward in the *vajrabandha* mudrā, opening them five *cun*, one *cun*, and three *cun* respectively.
The mantra for making offerings is as follows:
*Namo samanta-vajrāya hūṃ vikiri vidhūnaya hūṃ.* Next, bind the seal of the supreme flavor (*rasottama-mudrā*):

with the left and right hands in the inner-bound position (*antarmuṣṭi*), extend the two wind-fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) straight and firm at their middle joints, crossing them like the horns of a water buffalo at their tips.
The mantra for offering is:
Namaḥ vighnāntakāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Next is the Amṛtārāja-mudrā.
The two fingers on the left and right, representing water and fire, are both formed into the shape of jewels.
The two empty spaces, each measuring two finger-widths, have pillars between them that stand as straight as two upright shafts.

Furthermore, one reaches the great suffering of death;
moreover, through the practice of the Dharma with a pure mind, all dharmas are fully accomplished,
and no further doubt remains.
If one produces images and the like,
and the artisan desires to obtain much [recompense],
he will immediately receive the body of a great serpent in this very life.
All six sense faculties are incomplete;
they are constantly afflicted by suffering and eventually face death.
Furthermore, whether one occasionally offers sincere devotion with flowers and incense, or does not do so, one nonetheless accumulates meritorious karma through such actions.

merit and virtue will not fail to be accomplished.

the merit of the Dharma will not be realized;
throughout birth after birth, they shall not encounter the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha.
They constantly follow the paths of evil and the hells.
If they bestow teachings upon disciples with malicious intent who do not observe the precepts, the Dharma will be extinguished without remainder.
This Dharma is a rare phenomenon in this world.

one should perform this maṇḍala ritual;
it must not be transmitted to anyone else.
If it is transmitted to many, it will result in great evil, obstacles, difficulties, and the loss of the benefits of the Dharma.
If one possesses the aforementioned eight methods of the "Tusk" (*daṃṣṭrā*) correspondence,
upon attaining them, one’s status shall be equal to that of a king.

At that time, the King of Vināyakas, the Ten Rākṣasīs, the Scattering-Finger Great General, Vajrapāṇi Guhyapati, the Mahābala, and all the various great and small yakṣa generals, ghosts, and spirits [gathered].
"I have understood what Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, and the others said regarding the single aspect of *śamatha* and the ten hands;
we shall become yakṣa generals included among those who serve as messengers."
Thus we have always followed the Great King in performing his affairs and have all attained the name of Vaiśravaṇa.
At that time, if King Vināyaka and General Yūnū can understand this Dharani-Dharmamudrā of Liberation, they will certainly obtain the Seal of Entreaty.
The two water and earth elements stand interlaced;
the two fire and wind elements each join side by side.
Above the right fire and wind, and above the left fire and wind, are the two spaces.
Coming and going from the sound *ha*.
The mantra is:
Oṃ bhagavati amṛte khaḍgaye svāhā. This is the seal for the ten rākṣasīs and others.
The two earth-mudrās stand as water-forks;
the two fire-mudrās form triangles facing the corners of the mandala;

Join the two hands in *añjali*.

"Oṃ va-sa-ra hūṃ e-he-ki-su-bhaḥ. This is the seal for all spirits and deities (*sarva-bhūta*).
Join the two hands in *añjali* and strike them downward upon the altar.

Form a fist with the left hand and snap the fingers of the right hand seven times.

When making offerings, place three portions of black rice upon the altar and scatter white flower petals below them.
In accordance with one's mental vows,
one is able to make requests and take oaths,

we, the twenty-eight divisions of yakṣa generals and the rest,
shall constantly protect that person.

may all those afflicted by ghostly matters think only of us.
